title: The Cocktail Party Effect
objective: After this level you can explain selective attention and why your own name cuts through a noisy room.
summary: Selective attention follows one voice and tunes out the rest, yet about a third of people catch their own name in a message they are ignoring.

cards.headline: At a loud party, you follow one conversation. Then someone says your name.
cards.body: You weren't listening to them. So how did your name get through the noise?

cards.headline: One voice at a time
cards.body: Selective attention is the ability to pick out certain things to process while ignoring distractions. In a 1953 paper, Colin Cherry coined the term "cocktail-party problem" and took it into the lab: listeners heard a different message in each ear and repeated one aloud as they heard it, a task called shadowing. They could say little about what the ignored ear heard. Many didn't notice when it switched from English to German.

cards.headline: Your name breaks through
cards.body: If the ignored ear were truly shut off, your name couldn't get through either. Yet in Moray's 1959 study and a 1995 repeat by Wood and Cowan, about 33 percent of people reported hearing their own name in the message they were ignoring. Anne Treisman proposed an explanation: ignored information is turned down, not blocked, so something as meaningful as your name can still slip past.

cards.fact: In a 2021 replication, 29 percent noticed their own name. Unexpected words rarely got through.
cards.context: The study was preregistered, and the name effect held. And the people who caught their name tended to score lower on working-memory tests, which researchers read as more trouble blocking out distracting information.

cards.headline: Cocktail party
learned: Selective attention: follow one voice, ignore the rest
Cherry (1953): the ignored ear's content is mostly lost
About a third still catch their own name
Treisman: ignored input is turned down, not off

questions.prompt: In Colin Cherry's shadowing experiments, what did many listeners fail to notice in the ignored ear?

options.label: That a message was playing at all
options.rationale: They knew speech was there; they missed its content.

options.label: That it switched from English to German
That their own ear had been repeating it
options.rationale: They repeated the other ear's message.

options.label: That the music had stopped
options.rationale: The ignored ear carried speech, not music.

questions.explanation: Listeners shadowing one ear could say little about the other, and many missed a switch from English to German.

questions.prompt: How did Anne Treisman explain hearing your own name in a message you are ignoring?

options.label: The ignored ear is completely blocked
options.rationale: Then the name couldn't get through at all.

options.label: People secretly listen to both ears equally
options.rationale: Shadowers know little of the ignored message.

options.label: Ignored input is turned down, not off
Names are spoken more loudly than other words
options.rationale: The explanation is about meaning, not volume.

questions.explanation: Treisman proposed that ignored information is weakened rather than blocked, so highly meaningful words like your name can still get through.

questions.prompt: About a third of people reported hearing their name in the ignored message. Which kind of evidence from Level 1 is that?

options.label: A biological signal
options.rationale: No body signal was measured here.

options.label: A case study of one person

questions.explanation: People told the researchers what they had heard: a self-report, one of the observable measures Level 1 listed.
